body.statement: For every \(\vartheta\in\mathcal F_B(p)\) in the no-selection overlap satisfying \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm K}(P_{\vartheta})\), the simultaneous equations in the proof of Kawakami (2021), Theorem 1 on pages 12135--12137 identify \(\omega_0^{\mathrm K}\) and \(\omega_1^{\mathrm K}\). If \(\mathcal T_B(p)\) is a singleton, its atlas value agrees with \(\tau(\vartheta)=\phi_{\mathrm K}(\omega_0^{\mathrm K},\omega_1^{\mathrm K})\). Kawakami's identified scope is the four joint probabilities of binary potential-outcome types, together with their treatment-conditional weights used for PN and PS, under Figure 2(b), equation (2), and Theorem 1(i)--(iii). For the single explicit selected boundary datum \((p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\), \(\mathcal F_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\ne\varnothing\) and \(\mathcal T_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})=\{(1/2,1/2)\}\), but \(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) is singular for each \(x\): because \(\mathcal W=\{w_1,w_2,w_3\}\), its first column is the sum of its last three columns. Thus this legal selected response-cycle law violates the named invertibility assumption in Kawakami's Theorem 1(i) while remaining classified by the atlas; this is a strict scope separation, not a subsumption claim.
body.justification: This supporting theorem records the exact no-selection IV-plus-proxy overlap and a one-law separation from Kawakami's regular invertibility domain.
body.gap: Kawakami (2021), Figure 2(b), equation (2), Theorem 1(i)--(iii), and its appendix identify all four response-type probabilities under invertible proxy-loading and observable blocks plus cross-treatment separation, but do not classify selected or singular response-cycle fibers.
body.consumer: IV-plus-proxy analysts can audit agreement on Kawakami-regular laws and recognize a concrete selected boundary law for which the regular matrix method is unavailable but the atlas still returns an exact certificate.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(\vartheta\in\mathcal F_B(p)\) in the stated no-selection overlap and suppose \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm K}(P_{\vartheta})\).  The cited result \(\mathrm{lem:kawakami\text{-}iv\text{-}proxy\text{-}identification}\) identifies the two conditional response-type vectors \(\omega_0^{\mathrm K}\) and \(\omega_1^{\mathrm K}\) by the simultaneous equations in Kawakami's proof.  In the order \((00,01,10,11)\), response consistency implies that \((X,Y)=(1,1)\) admits exactly types \(01\) and \(11\), whereas \((X,Y)=(0,0)\) admits exactly types \(00\) and \(01\).  Because \(S=1\) almost surely and the selected cells are positive, the probabilities of these two conditioning events are positive.  Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{PN}(\vartheta)
 &=\frac{\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,2}}
         {\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,2}+\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,4}},\\
\operatorname{PS}(\vartheta)
 &=\frac{\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,2}}
         {\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,1}+\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is exactly
\[
\tau(\vartheta)=\phi_{\mathrm K}(\omega_0^{\mathrm K},\omega_1^{\mathrm K}). \tag{8}
\]
If \(\mathcal T_B(p)\) is a singleton, it contains \(\tau(\vartheta)\) by definition.  The full-rigidity theorem makes the atlas return its unique element, which equals (8).

It remains to verify the separate scope witness.  Every row of \(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) has the form
\[
\bigl(1,b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_1),b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_2),b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_3)\bigr).
\]
Since \(b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}\in\Delta_{\{w_1,w_2,w_3\}}\), the last three entries sum to one.  Thus, for either \(x\), the first column of \(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) is the sum of its last three columns, and \(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) is singular.  The already established \(\mathrm{thm:experimental\text{-}proxy\text{-}reduction\text{-}and\text{-}boundary\text{-}separation}\) gives
\[
\mathcal F_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\ne\varnothing,
\qquad
\mathcal T_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})=\{(1/2,1/2)\}.
\]
Hence the datum is legally classified by the atlas but violates the named invertibility premise of Kawakami's Theorem 1(i).  This proves strict scope separation for this law, without asserting that either theorem subsumes the other.
